statements.text: Artificial intelligence is a broad field of methods for getting computers to perform tasks that normally need human judgment.
statements.explanation: AI is a field, not a single product. It spans rule-based systems, statistical learning, and modern neural networks. When someone says a product uses AI, the useful follow-up is which method and for what task.

statements.text: Machine learning and artificial intelligence are two names for exactly the same thing.
statements.explanation: Machine learning is one approach within AI: systems that improve from data rather than from hand-written rules. Older AI includes expert systems and search methods that learn nothing. Most AI you meet today is machine learning, which is why the words blur.

statements.text: A machine learning model is a set of numbers tuned on examples so that it maps inputs to useful outputs.
statements.explanation: Training adjusts millions or billions of numeric weights until the model's outputs match the examples well. The finished model is those weights plus the recipe for applying them. There is no stored list of answers inside.

statements.text: An algorithm is a kind of AI, so any software that uses an algorithm is using AI.
statements.explanation: An algorithm is any step-by-step procedure; sorting a list or computing a sum uses one. AI methods are algorithms, but most algorithms are not AI. The label fits when the system learns from data or reasons over knowledge, not merely because it computes.

statements.text: A large language model is trained to predict the next piece of text given the text before it.
statements.explanation: That single objective, applied across enormous amounts of text, is what produces the ability to answer questions, draft documents, and follow instructions. Every reply is built one predicted token at a time.

statements.text: A language model stores a copy of every document it was trained on and looks answers up in that copy.
statements.explanation: Training compresses patterns from text into weights; the documents themselves are not kept inside the model. It can reproduce common passages it saw often, but it has no library to search unless a retrieval feature is attached.

statements.text: Generative AI refers to systems that produce new content such as text, images, audio, or code.
statements.explanation: The word generative marks the output: something new in the style of the training data, rather than a label or a score. Chat assistants, image generators, and code assistants all belong to this group.

statements.text: Every AI system is generative, so all AI makes things up by nature.
statements.explanation: Many AI systems only classify or rank: a spam filter labels, a fraud model scores, a recommender orders. They produce decisions, not prose, and cannot invent a sentence. Hallucination is a property of generative systems in particular.

statements.text: A neural network is a layered arrangement of simple numeric operations whose weights are learned from data.
statements.explanation: Each layer transforms its input with multiplications and additions followed by a simple nonlinear step. Stacking many layers lets the network represent complex patterns. The name comes from a loose analogy to neurons, not from copying a brain.

statements.text: Neural networks work the same way a human brain does.
statements.explanation: The analogy inspired the name, but the mechanisms differ: artificial networks use dense matrix arithmetic trained by gradient descent, with no biology, chemistry, or embodiment. Useful intuition, misleading claim.

statements.text: Deep learning means using neural networks with many layers.
statements.explanation: Deep refers to the number of layers, not to depth of understanding. Many layers let a network build up features step by step, which is why deep models handle images, speech, and language so well.

statements.text: A model that performs one task well, such as recognising faces, can do any other task equally well.
statements.explanation: Most trained models are narrow: a face recogniser knows nothing about language. Large language models are broader because text covers many tasks, but even they fail outside what their training supports. Match the tool to the task.

statements.text: The term artificial general intelligence refers to a hypothetical system that matches humans across most intellectual tasks.
statements.explanation: AGI is a goal and a debate, not a product. Current systems are strong in some areas and weak in others. When a headline claims AGI has arrived, look for the definition being used and the evidence behind it.

statements.text: Chatbots are a recent invention that only became possible with modern neural networks.
statements.explanation: Rule-based chat programs date back decades; one of the earliest matched patterns in typed sentences and reflected them back. What is new is fluency and breadth, which came from large language models trained on vast text.

statements.text: Training a model and using a trained model are two separate phases.
statements.explanation: Training adjusts the weights over many passes through data and usually takes significant compute. Inference, the use phase, runs the fixed model on a new input. Your chat message is inference; it does not retrain anything.

statements.text: A model keeps learning from every user who talks to it, getting smarter in real time.
statements.explanation: Deployed models have fixed weights. Providers may collect conversations to train a future version, under their stated policy, but the model answering you now does not change as you type. Memory features store notes; they do not retrain the model.

statements.text: Fine-tuning adjusts an existing model with additional examples instead of training from scratch.
statements.explanation: Starting from a pretrained model and nudging its weights on a smaller, focused dataset is far cheaper than training anew. It is how general models are shaped for a domain, a tone, or a task.

statements.text: Prompting a model and fine-tuning a model change the model in the same way.
statements.explanation: A prompt changes the input for one request and leaves the weights alone; fine-tuning changes the weights for every future request. Prompting is reversible and instant; fine-tuning is a build step with lasting effects.

statements.text: A prompt is the text you give a language model to shape what it produces.
statements.explanation: Everything in the request, including instructions, examples, and pasted material, is the prompt. Because the model predicts from that text, the way you write it is the main control you have over the answer.

statements.text: A model's parameters are the settings a user adjusts in the app's preferences screen.
statements.explanation: Parameters are the learned weights inside the model, fixed after training and numbering in the millions or billions. User-facing settings such as temperature or length are separate controls on how the fixed model is sampled.

statements.text: Classification is a common AI task where the system assigns an input to one of a set of categories.
statements.explanation: Spam or not spam, which digit is in the image, which language is this text: each is classification. It is the workhorse of practical AI and needs no text generation at all.

statements.text: If a system was built with AI, it must have been given a goal and figured out how to reach it on its own.
statements.explanation: Most AI systems are trained for a narrow objective chosen by people and operate within fixed software. Autonomous goal pursuit describes a small class of agent systems, and even those act inside limits their builders set.

statements.text: Training data is the collection of examples a model learns from.
statements.explanation: The data sets the ceiling: a model cannot learn a pattern it never saw, and it absorbs the gaps and skews of its examples. Questions about what a model can do often come down to what it was trained on.

statements.text: More training data always produces a better model regardless of what the data contains.
statements.explanation: Quantity helps only when quality holds. Duplicated, mislabeled, or off-topic data can make a model worse. Curating data is a large part of building a good model, which is why data work is a profession of its own.

statements.text: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text or an image.
statements.explanation: Models turn inputs into vectors so that similar things sit near each other in number space. Search, recommendation, and retrieval compare these vectors. The numbers are not readable by people, but their distances are useful.

statements.text: A computer vision model sees a picture the way a person does, as objects and scenes.
statements.explanation: The model receives a grid of pixel numbers and learns statistical patterns that correlate with labels. It has no notion of a scene unless trained to output one, and it can be fooled by patterns a person would ignore.

statements.text: Speech recognition, machine translation, and image generation are all applications of machine learning.
statements.explanation: Each maps an input to an output learned from paired examples: sound to text, one language to another, a description to pixels. The methods share a family even though the products look unrelated.

statements.text: AI systems understand the meaning of words the way people do.
statements.explanation: Models represent words as numbers shaped by how words occur together. That captures a lot of usage, enough to be useful, without the lived grounding people have. The practical lesson is to check outputs rather than assume comprehension.

statements.text: A model's output for a prompt can be shaped by randomness in how the next piece of text is chosen.
statements.explanation: Sampling picks among likely next tokens rather than always taking the top one, which is why answers vary between runs. A lower randomness setting makes outputs more repeatable; it does not make them more correct.

statements.text: A bigger model is always more accurate than a smaller one on every task.
statements.explanation: Size tends to help on broad tasks, but a small model trained for a specific job often beats a large general one on that job, at lower cost. Evaluate on your task rather than trusting size.

statements.text: An AI agent is a system that uses a model to choose actions, such as calling tools, in a loop toward a goal.
statements.explanation: The model proposes a step, software runs it, the result goes back to the model, and the loop continues. Agents extend what a chat model can do and add new ways to fail, which is why limits and review matter.

statements.text: Open-source AI means the model has no restrictions and can do anything a closed model cannot.
statements.explanation: Open release means the weights or code are published under a license, which can still carry conditions. Capability is a separate matter; open and closed models each cover a range. Read the license and the evaluation, not the label.

statements.text: Rule-based systems that follow hand-written if-then logic were an early form of AI.
statements.explanation: Expert systems encoded human knowledge as rules and were used in medicine and industry decades ago. They did not learn, which limited them, but they are part of the field's history and still run in some places.

statements.text: The word model in AI means a physical replica of a brain built from circuits.
statements.explanation: In AI, a model is a mathematical function with learned parameters, stored as software and run on ordinary processors. No circuitry mimics a brain; the word is used in the same sense as a statistical model.

statements.text: Inference is the name for running a trained model on a new input to get an output.
statements.explanation: Each chat reply, each image label, and each translation is an inference call. Providers price and scale this phase separately from training, which is why usage costs are quoted per request or per token.

statements.text: A chatbot and a language model are the same thing.
statements.explanation: The model is the engine; the chatbot is the product around it, with a system prompt, safety filters, memory features, tools, and an interface. Two products on the same model can behave quite differently.

statements.text: A system prompt is hidden instruction text that a product gives the model before your message.
statements.explanation: Products set tone, rules, and persona in a system prompt the user usually does not see. It shapes every reply, which is one reason the same question gets different answers from different assistants built on similar models.

statements.text: Because AI runs on computers, its answers are objective and free of human influence.
statements.explanation: People choose the data, the objective, the rules, and the tuning. Human influence is built in at every stage, which is why the same model can be shaped toward very different behavior. Objectivity has to be checked, not assumed.

statements.text: Hallucination is the term for a model producing confident output that is false or unsupported.
statements.explanation: The word is loose but widely used. It covers invented citations, wrong dates, and made-up details stated plainly. Knowing the term helps you ask the right question of any output: what supports this.

statements.text: Once a model is accurate on a benchmark, it will be equally accurate on your own task.
statements.explanation: Benchmarks measure a fixed set of questions that may look nothing like your work. Models also sometimes see benchmark material during training. Test on a sample of your own inputs before trusting a score.
